nameStory: The "spotted" in spotted grass moth comes from the distinctive dark spots scattered across its pale wings, like tiny ink drops on parchment. It's also called the yellow snout-moth because of its yellowish coloration and the way its elongated mouthparts (called palps) project forward like a little snout.
description: The spotted grass moth is a small, delicate moth with a wingspan of just 15-19 millimeters - about the size of your thumbnail. Its pale yellow to cream-colored wings are decorated with small dark spots and subtle patterns that help it blend in with dried grasses. This tiny moth belongs to a large family that includes some of our most dramatic moths, though this species opts for understated elegance over flashy colors. When at rest, it holds its wings in a tent-like position over its slender body.

idTips.label: Wing spots
idTips.description: Look for small, dark spots scattered across pale yellow or cream-colored wings - they're irregular and give the moth a speckled appearance like tiny paint spatters

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small moth with wings spanning only 15-19mm - smaller than a quarter and easily overlooked among grass stems

idTips.label: Snout-like palps
idTips.description: Notice the elongated mouthparts that project forward from the head like a tiny beak or snout, giving it a distinctive profile

idTips.label: Wing position at rest
idTips.description: When resting, holds wings in a triangular tent shape over the body rather than spread flat

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Overall pale yellowish or cream background color with subtle darker markings that create a mottled, grass-like camouflage

habitat: Look for spotted grass moths in grassy areas throughout New England, from meadows and prairies to lawn edges and weedy fields. They're particularly common in areas with diverse native grasses, as these provide food for their caterpillars. You'll find them from sea level to mountain meadows, anywhere grasses grow abundantly.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, when you might spot them fluttering weakly among grass stems in the evening hours.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs through June, July, and early August when adults are most numerous and actively mating. Look for them at dusk near outdoor lights.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down by late August, though you might occasionally find worn specimens into early September.
seasonality.winter: The species overwinters in an immature stage, likely as caterpillars or pupae hidden among grass roots and debris.

funFact: Despite being called a "grass moth," the spotted grass moth is actually more closely related to dramatic tiger moths and underwing moths than to the grass moths you might expect - it's a perfect example of how common names can be misleading in the moth world!
confusionNotes: Many small, pale moths can look similar, but the combination of distinct dark spots on pale wings and the prominent snout-like palps sets this species apart. Remember: "Spotted snout in the grass" - if you see both the spots and the protruding mouthparts, you've found your moth.
contextualKnowledge: The name "grass moth" is used for several unrelated moth groups, which can confuse beginners. True grass moths belong to the family Crambidae, while our spotted grass moth is in Erebidae. This naming overlap reflects how early naturalists grouped moths by habitat rather than evolutionary relationships.
compareHints: The spotted grass moth is the only member of its genus Rivula found in New England, making it unique in the region. Among similar small Erebidae moths, it's distinguished by its particular combination of pale coloration, distinct spotting pattern, and prominent snout-like palps. Most other small moths in this family either lack the clear spots or have different wing shapes and resting postures.
